paragraphs.text: Building Enough Safety to Stay Present
Somatic Experiencing

Somatic Experiencing is something I reach for when merely approaching the material sends my body over the edge. There is sensation, orientation, impulse, defensive response, and pacing to work with. I do not need the whole story first.

Titration and pendulation make sense because there is no prize for beating trauma in a fight. I touch as much activation as I can honestly tolerate, notice what happens, and come back toward something steadier. Some people spend three to six months building that capacity. Severe developmental trauma can take longer. I use that as orientation, not a countdown, and I see no reason for somebody already stable with a clear target to wait out arbitrary months before adding focused trauma work.
Trauma-Sensitive / Restorative Yoga

By yoga I do not mean power yoga, hot yoga, or somebody announcing, “Open your hips and release your trauma.” I mean slow and choice-based: trauma-sensitive yoga, restorative yoga, gentle somatic yoga, maybe very gentle yin. For yin I want props, shorter holds, and an easy exit.
The instructions should sound more like:

“You might try…”
“You can keep your eyes open.”
“Come out of the shape whenever you want.”
“Is this useful, neutral, or too much?”
“There can be several right versions. Pick the one that fits your body.”

Intense stretching, breath retention, forced breathwork, aggressive hip opening, long passive holds, hands-on adjustments without clear consent, pushing through because suffering is supposedly therapeutic—I am not recommending any of that. Once I can't choose, it isn't the practice I mean anymore.
Gentle Shaking / TRE
Here I mean a little shaking. Not an attempt to blast trauma out of my body.

Basic TRE, very light neurogenic tremoring, gentle shaking while standing, even a short bit of playful movement may be plenty. Once it feels compulsive, frightening, dissociative, or difficult to stop, it is no longer what I mean by gentle.

paragraphs.text: Building Enough Safety to Stay Present
Somatic Experiencing

Somatic Experiencing is what I reach for when merely getting near the material sends my body over the edge. I can begin with a sensation, orient to the room, notice an impulse or defensive response, and slow down the pace. The whole story can wait.

The useful move is not to beat trauma in a fight. I touch only as much activation as I can honestly tolerate, see what happens, then come back toward something steadier. That is titration and pendulation in practice. Some people spend three to six months building that ability, and severe developmental trauma can take longer. I treat those numbers as orientation, not a countdown. If somebody is already stable and has one clear target, I see no reason to make them wait out arbitrary months before adding focused trauma work.
Trauma-Sensitive / Restorative Yoga

Power yoga, hot yoga, and somebody announcing, “Open your hips and release your trauma,” are not what I mean here. I mean the slow stuff: trauma-sensitive yoga, restorative yoga, gentle somatic yoga, maybe very gentle yin with props, shorter holds, and an easy way out.
Most of the useful instructions are permissions:

“You might try…”
“You can keep your eyes open.”
“Come out of the shape whenever you want.”
“Is this useful, neutral, or too much?”
“There can be several right versions. Pick the one that fits your body.”

I leave out intense stretching, breath retention, forced breathwork, aggressive hip opening, long passive holds, hands-on adjustments without clear consent, and pushing through because suffering is supposedly therapeutic. Once I cannot choose, it is no longer the practice I mean.
Gentle Shaking / TRE

The shaking here is also the small version. Basic TRE, very light neurogenic tremoring, gentle shaking while standing, or a short bit of playful movement may be enough. I am not trying to blast trauma out of my body. If it becomes compulsive, frightening, dissociative, or hard to stop, I have gone past gentle.

paragraphs.text: Building Enough Safety to Stay Present
Somatic Experiencing

If getting near the material knocks me out of myself, I don't start with the story. I can feel what is happening in my body, look around the room, catch an impulse to run or push away or freeze, and slow the whole thing down. Sensation, orientation, impulse, defensive response, pacing—that is already plenty to work with.

I go in a little and come back. Then again. The technical words are titration and pendulation, but the point is not to overwhelm myself while pretending that overwhelm is healing. Some people need three to six months to get good at staying with activation and returning to something steadier. Severe developmental trauma can take longer. I use those numbers for orientation, not as a calendar I have to obey. If somebody is already stable and has one clear target, I would add focused trauma work sooner.
Trauma-Sensitive / Restorative Yoga

Power yoga? No. Hot yoga? No. Somebody announcing, “Open your hips and release your trauma”? Also no. I mean the slow, choice-based kinds: trauma-sensitive yoga, restorative yoga, gentle somatic yoga, maybe very gentle yin with props, shorter holds, and an easy way out.
The teacher should keep giving the choice back:

“You might try…”
“You can keep your eyes open.”
“Come out of the shape whenever you want.”
“Is this useful, neutral, or too much?”
“There can be several right versions. Pick the one that fits your body.”

No intense stretching, breath retention, forced breathwork, aggressive hip opening, long passive holds, or hands-on adjustments without clear consent. And no pushing through because suffering is supposedly therapeutic. If I cannot leave the shape, change it, or say no, I come out.
Gentle Shaking / TRE

A little shaking can be enough. Basic TRE, a very light neurogenic tremor, standing and shaking gently, a short bit of playful movement. I am not trying to blast trauma out of my body. Compulsive, frightening, dissociative, hard to stop—any of those means I went too far.
